title: Feynman Meets Turing: The Curse of Quantum Universality
authors: Yannik N. Böck, Holger Boche, Frank H. P. Fitzek
abstract: We consider a formal model of quantum circuit description languages (QCDLs) in which semantically meaningful programs correspond to computable unitary matrices. We show that any semantically universal QCDL -- that is, any QCDL able to describe all computable unitary matrices, which in turn form the set of matrices we can meaningfully represent on digital hardware -- cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful descriptions. In particular, no such language admits a compiler that reliably recognizes all valid program descriptions. This result stands in contrast to classical programming languages. While compilation in languages such as C or C++ may itself involve non-terminating computations, the set of semantically meaningful programs remains recursively enumerable, since successful compilation provides a witness of validity. The essential difference lies in the nature of the semantic domains: classical languages describe partial recursive functions, whereas QCDLs describe total unitary operators. Our analysis establishes a fundamental limitation of quantum circuit description languages and highlights a structural distinction between classical and quantum models of computation at the level of formal language theory.
summary: This paper proves a fundamental limitation: any quantum language capable of describing all possible computable unitary operations cannot have its valid programs recognized by a semi-decidable compiler. This structural difference arises because the semantic domain of quantum circuits consists only of total unitary operators, unlike classical languages which allow for partial computations.
main_problem: To establish a fundamental limitation on Quantum Circuit Description Languages (QCDLs) regarding their formal language theory properties, contrasting them with classical programming languages.
main_result: Any semantically universal QCDL cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful descriptions, implying no reliable compiler can exist for such a language.
method: Formal analysis using recursion theory and computable analysis to compare the computability properties of classical vs. quantum semantic domains.
model_or_system: The model involves formalizing QCDLs where semantics are defined by computable unitary matrices, contrasting this total domain with the partial function descriptions of classical languages.
key_observables: The set of semantically meaningful program descriptions; whether this set is semi-decidable or recursively enumerable.
important_parameters: Fixed dimension N >= 2 for semantic universality; computable unitary matrices ($\mathcal{U}_{\mu}$).
main_assumptions: The result holds assuming the QCDL aims to describe all computable unitary matrices (semantic universality).
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate quantum computing in the circuit model and a 'Matrix Quantum Computer' setup, detailing how high-level descriptions map to unitary matrix elements.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general computability theory concepts to define QCDLs, contrasts their total semantic domain with classical partial functions, and culminates in proving that universal QCDLs violate semi-decidability.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical constraint on the formal expressiveness of quantum programming languages, which is foundational knowledge for anyone designing or analyzing quantum hardware control software.
